passages.title: Borrowed Letters: How the Alphabet Travelled
passages.passage:
A. Consider the letter you are reading now. Its shape was settled long before any language you speak existed, and its journey to this page passed through the hands of people who would not have recognised a single word of English. Most writing systems that humans have devised record meanings or syllables; the alphabet, by contrast, records sounds so small that they cannot be pronounced on their own. That was a strange idea, and it appears to have been invented only once.

B. The earliest trace of it lies in a set of scratched marks found on rock faces and mining tools in a desert region, dating to roughly four thousand years ago. Whoever made them was not a professional scribe. Scribes of that era were trained in an elaborate script of hundreds of pictorial signs, and they had every reason to keep it complicated, since their livelihood depended on the rarity of the skill. The desert marks instead borrowed a couple of dozen of those pictures and used each one to stand for the first sound of its name. A drawing of a house no longer meant "house"; it meant the consonant with which the word for house began. Not until the trick had been simplified in this way could a labourer, rather than a court official, hope to learn to write.

C. The system travelled north with traders, and it is to those traders that the word "alphabet" ultimately owes its first two syllables. Being merchants rather than priests, they cared about speed, and under their pens the pictures were worn down to abstract strokes, much as a coin loses its detail through handling. Crucially, they wrote only consonants. A reader supplied the vowels from context, which works well enough for a language whose vowels are largely predictable, and rather badly for one whose are not.

D. Herein lay the problem for the next borrowers, who spoke a language in which vowels carried real weight. Their solution was less a stroke of genius than a happy accident. Several of the inherited letters stood for throat sounds that did not exist in the new language and so were, in effect, unemployed. Rather than discard them, the adopters reassigned them to vowels. Had those sounds happened to exist in the borrowing language, we might still be writing without an A or an E. It was this modified set that later peoples inherited, turned in another direction, gave new names and, over several centuries, carried across a continent.

E. What is striking, looking back over the whole story, is how little of it was designed. No committee sat down to invent a writing system for the masses. Each step was taken by people solving an immediate, local problem: how to mark a tool, how to record a cargo, how to write a name that the borrowed letters could not spell. The alphabet's efficiency, so often praised, is the residue of thousands of such small acts of laziness and improvisation. The one deliberate decision in its history, that of the desert miners who first let a picture stand for a sound, was made by people whose names no letter ever recorded.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) explains why professional scribes had no interest in making writing simpler?
questions.explanation: Section B says the scribes 'had every reason to keep it complicated, since their livelihood depended on the rarity of the skill'.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) describes letters changing shape as a result of frequent use?
questions.explanation: Section C: under the traders' pens 'the pictures were worn down to abstract strokes, much as a coin loses its detail through handling'.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) describes a feature of the alphabet that arose because certain letters had nothing to do?
questions.explanation: Section D: letters for throat sounds absent from the new language were 'in effect, unemployed', so the adopters 'reassigned them to vowels'.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) argues that the alphabet was not the product of planning?
questions.explanation: Section E: 'how little of it was designed' and 'No committee sat down to invent a writing system for the masses'.

questions.q: Which statement best sums up the writer's view of the alphabet's history?
options: It was a series of practical shortcuts by ordinary people rather than a deliberate invention.
It was the achievement of a small class of highly trained scribes.
It developed separately in several regions before the versions merged.
It has changed so much that its origins can no longer be traced.
questions.explanation: The passage repeatedly stresses accident and improvisation: labourers, traders in a hurry, a 'happy accident' with unused letters, and 'small acts of laziness and improvisation'.

questions.q: What can be inferred about the spoken language of the traders in section C?
options: It had no vowel sounds at all.
Its vowels could usually be worked out from the surrounding consonants.
It contained more consonants than any later language.
It was used mainly for religious ceremonies.
questions.explanation: The traders wrote only consonants, and the writer says this 'works well enough for a language whose vowels are largely predictable' — since they used it successfully, their language must have been of that type. The passage never says they lacked vowels.

questions.q: In section E, the word 'residue' is closest in meaning to:
options: a reward given for hard work
a mistake that was later corrected
what is left behind after a process
a formal record kept for the future
questions.explanation: The alphabet's efficiency is described as the 'residue' — what remains — of thousands of small acts, not something anyone aimed at.

questions.q: The people who introduced vowel letters set out deliberately to improve the writing system.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Section D calls their solution 'less a stroke of genius than a happy accident': they simply reused letters that had no sound to represent.

passages.title: Hives Above the Traffic
passages.passage:
For most of the last century, anyone who wished to keep bees was assumed to need a field, or at the very least a large garden well away from the neighbours. [1] Hives now sit on hotel roofs, in school courtyards and behind the wheelie bins of terraced houses, and city councils that once banned them compete to advertise how many they host.

The appeal is easy to understand. Bees ask for little space, they are quiet, and they produce something you can spread on toast. There is also a widespread belief that the city is, against all expectation, a rather good place for them. Suburban gardens, railway embankments and municipal parks offer a variety of flowers that a field of a single crop cannot match, and the plants in them are far less likely to have been sprayed. [2] Several studies have found that colonies on urban rooftops come through the winter at least as well as their rural cousins, and sometimes better.

Yet the story has a complication that the brochures rarely mention. The honeybee is a livestock animal, and like any livestock it competes for food. [3] Each of those colonies sends out tens of thousands of foragers, and every flower they strip is one that a wild bee cannot visit. Since wild bees, of which most temperate countries have several hundred species, neither live in hives nor make honey that anyone harvests, nobody counts them, and their decline goes unnoticed until it is well advanced.

The arithmetic is unforgiving. Ecologists who have measured the nectar available in a typical city district estimate that it can support a certain density of colonies before the foragers begin to go hungry. [4] In several capitals that ceiling has already been passed several times over, with the predictable result that honey yields per hive are falling even as the number of hives climbs.

None of this means that the rooftop hive is a mistake. It means that its benefit has been misdescribed. [5] What it does is bring the people who install it into daily contact with the question of what is flowering, where, and for how long, and that question, followed to its conclusion, leads not to more hives but to more flowers. The beekeepers who understand this tend, after a season or two, to spend less on equipment and more on seed. Their neighbours' balconies fill with lavender and thyme; the wild bees, whom nobody invited, come back to feed. The hive, in the end, was never the point. It was the excuse.

A. A single city block may now house a dozen hives where a generation ago it held none.
B. Whatever good it does is done not by the bees but by the beekeeper.
C. That assumption has collapsed in the space of a couple of decades.
D. Rural beekeepers, by contrast, have always relied on a single crop for most of their yield.
E. That figure is low, and it does not rise simply because a new hive has been installed.
F. Cities are also a degree or two warmer, so something is in bloom for more of the year.
G. Most of these species are protected by law, and harming them can carry a fine.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [1]?
questions.explanation: 'That assumption' picks up the belief that beekeeping needs a field, and its collapse leads straight into the list of unlikely places hives now sit.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [2]?
questions.explanation: 'Cities are also…' adds a further advantage (warmth, longer flowering) to the list of reasons the city suits bees, before the studies that confirm it. D contrasts rural keepers but the paragraph is about why cities are good, not about rural yields.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [3]?
questions.explanation: 'Each of those colonies' needs a preceding mention of many colonies in one place, which A supplies with 'a dozen hives' on one block.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [4]?
questions.explanation: 'That figure' refers to the estimated density of colonies a district can support, and 'that ceiling' in the next sentence refers back to E's fixed limit.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [5]?
questions.explanation: B explains how the benefit has been 'misdescribed' — it belongs to the beekeeper, not the bees — and 'What it does is bring the people…' then develops that idea.

questions.q: What is the writer's central claim about rooftop beekeeping?
options: Its real value lies in what it leads people to do rather than in the bees themselves.
It should be banned in cities where wild bees are declining.
It produces more honey than rural beekeeping because city flowers are unsprayed.
It has been oversold by councils but is harmless to other species.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph argues that the hive's benefit 'has been misdescribed': it matters because it turns its owner into someone who plants flowers — 'The hive… was never the point. It was the excuse.'

questions.q: What does the writer suggest about the falling honey yields in overcrowded cities?
options: They prove that urban bees are less healthy than rural ones.
They are mainly caused by pesticides used in municipal parks.
They will recover once councils stop advertising their hives.
They were foreseeable by anyone who had grasped the limit on available food.
questions.explanation: The writer calls the fall 'the predictable result' of passing the ceiling 'several times over': given fixed nectar and more hives, the outcome follows from 'unforgiving' arithmetic. The passage says urban bees overwinter as well as or better than rural ones, so B is contradicted.

questions.q: The phrase 'The arithmetic is unforgiving' means that the calculation:
options: changes from one season to the next
has rarely been published in full
leaves no room for argument or exception
is too difficult for most beekeepers to follow
questions.explanation: 'Unforgiving' describes something harsh that allows no escape; the nectar limit is fixed and exceeding it has an inevitable consequence.

passages.title: The Long Road from Laboratory to Arm
passages.passage:
A. A vaccine that reaches a clinic has already survived a process designed, at every stage, to kill it. This is not a figure of speech. The overwhelming majority of candidates that enter testing never leave it, and the ones that do have usually spent the better part of a decade being challenged, doubted and measured. The public tends to hear only about the final months, when a result is announced and a decision made. What precedes that announcement is far less visible and far more important.

B. Before a candidate goes anywhere near a human being, it must earn the right to do so in the laboratory and in animals. Researchers want to know two things: whether it provokes the immune system to respond at all, and whether that response comes at an unacceptable cost. A candidate that produces a splendid antibody count in mice but leaves them visibly unwell will go no further, however promising the count. Only when both questions have been answered to a regulator's satisfaction is permission given to move on, and the permission is narrow: it covers a small number of volunteers, a single dose, and nothing else.

C. Those first volunteers, rarely more than a few dozen, are healthy adults, and the question asked of them is not whether the vaccine works but whether it is safe enough to keep asking. Doses are increased slowly, one small group at a time, so that any problem reveals itself at the lowest level that causes it. Seldom does anything dramatic happen at this stage, precisely because the animal work has already filtered out the worst candidates; what emerges instead is a picture of the sore arms, mild fevers and headaches that are the price of provoking an immune system on purpose.

D. The decisive stage is the one that involves thousands of people and takes the longest. Half receive the candidate and half a placebo, and neither the volunteers nor the doctors examining them know which is which until the trial is over. The reason for this secrecy is not distrust of anyone's honesty. It is that people who believe themselves protected behave differently, and doctors who know which patient got the real thing may, without meaning to, judge a cough more leniently in one group than the other. Then the trial waits. Nothing can be concluded until enough participants have, in the ordinary course of their lives, encountered the disease, and the only way to shorten that wait is to run the trial where the disease is common. A vaccine tested during a lull in infections may take years to produce an answer; the same vaccine tested during an outbreak may produce one in months, with no corner cut.

E. Approval is not the end. Rare side effects, by definition, cannot show themselves among a few thousand people, so every vaccine in use is watched across the millions who receive it, and a signal that appears at that scale can pause a programme within days. Critics sometimes cite such pauses as evidence that the testing failed. The opposite is true. A system that could not detect an event affecting one person in a hundred thousand would be a system that had stopped looking.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) explains why doctors, as well as volunteers, must not know who received the vaccine?
questions.explanation: Section D: doctors who know 'may, without meaning to, judge a cough more leniently in one group than the other'.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) gives a reason why a candidate with impressive results might still be rejected?
questions.explanation: Section B: a candidate with 'a splendid antibody count in mice' that leaves them unwell 'will go no further, however promising the count'.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) corrects a mistaken interpretation of a programme being halted?
questions.explanation: Section E: critics cite pauses as evidence of failure, but 'The opposite is true' — a pause shows the system is still looking.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) describes the minor discomforts that early testing is expected to reveal?
questions.explanation: Section C lists 'the sore arms, mild fevers and headaches that are the price of provoking an immune system on purpose'.

questions.q: Why does the writer contrast a trial run during a lull with one run during an outbreak?
options: To explain why some vaccines are approved without a placebo group.
To suggest that outbreaks make results less reliable.
To show that a trial can be fast without any step being skipped.
To argue that trials should never be run while a disease is spreading.
questions.explanation: The point of the contrast is the final phrase: an outbreak trial 'may produce one in months, with no corner cut' — speed comes from how often participants meet the disease, not from lower standards.

questions.q: What does the writer imply about the public's understanding of how vaccines are tested?
options: It has improved since results began to be announced publicly.
It is deliberately kept incomplete by regulators.
It concentrates too heavily on animal experiments.
It is shaped by the shortest and least significant part of the process.
questions.explanation: Section A says the public 'tends to hear only about the final months', while 'what precedes that announcement is far less visible and far more important' — so their picture is built on the least important stage.

questions.q: In section D, 'judge a cough more leniently' means to judge it:
options: less strictly
more quickly
more carefully
less often
questions.explanation: 'Leniently' means with less severity; a doctor who expects a patient to be protected may treat a symptom as less serious than it is.

questions.q: Most of the candidates that fail do so during the animal stage.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The passage says most candidates fail somewhere, and that animal work filters out 'the worst', but it never says at which stage the majority are lost.

passages.title: Who Does the Car Decide to Hit?
passages.passage:
Ask a room of engineers what troubles them most about a car that drives itself and they will talk about sensors in fog, or software that has never seen a cow. Ask a room of philosophers and you will hear a different worry altogether. [1] Should it swerve into a wall and sacrifice its passenger, or hold its course and strike the people in the road? Versions of this dilemma have filled lecture halls and newspaper columns for a decade, and surveys have found, with tedious consistency, that most people want other people's cars to sacrifice their passengers while wanting their own car to protect them.

The engineers, for their part, find the question faintly ridiculous. [2] A car that finds itself choosing between two groups of victims has already failed, several seconds earlier, to do the one thing it was built to do, which is to notice the situation developing and slow down. Real crashes are rarely a clean choice between two evils; they are a muddle of partial information, in which the most valuable decision is almost always the dull one of braking sooner.

Yet the philosophers are not wrong that something has changed, even if they have located it in the wrong place. [3] When a human driver swerves, the choice is made in a fraction of a second by someone who will have to live with it. When a self-driving car swerves, the choice was made months earlier, in an office, by people who will never meet anyone involved, and it was made not once but for every car of that model, in every city, for as long as the software runs. What was a reflex has become a policy.

That shift raises questions that no lecture-hall dilemma captures. [4] The company will say the choice was made by the software; the programmers will say they followed a specification; the specification will turn out to have been written to satisfy a regulation whose authors were thinking about something else entirely. Responsibility, which once sat squarely in the driver's seat, has been distributed so widely that nobody appears to be holding any of it.

There is, too, a subtler difficulty. Every self-driving system is trained on records of how humans drive, and humans drive unequally. [5] A system that learns from such data will reproduce the pattern faithfully and at scale, and it will do so without any of the human driver's capacity to be embarrassed about it. Had the technology been introduced with these questions already answered, the debate might have been a short one. Instead, the questions were asked only once the cars were on the road, and the answers are being written, line by line, in code that very few people are permitted to read.

A. It assumes, they point out, a machine that has been paying no attention until the last possible moment.
B. If such a car strikes a pedestrian, who, exactly, is to blame?
C. Most passengers, in practice, never read the terms they agree to when they enter the vehicle.
D. Suppose, they say, that the brakes fail and a collision can no longer be avoided.
E. Insurance companies have so far declined to comment on any of these scenarios.
F. The novelty lies not in the decision itself but in when, where and by whom it is taken.
G. Drivers slow down more readily in some neighbourhoods than in others, and give more room to some pedestrians than to others.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [1]?
questions.explanation: D introduces the philosophers' scenario ('they say… the brakes fail'), and the next sentence asks what the car should then do.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [2]?
questions.explanation: A gives the engineers' objection ('they point out'): the dilemma assumes an inattentive machine, which the following sentence develops — such a car 'has already failed… to notice the situation developing'.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [3]?
questions.explanation: F names what has really changed — 'when, where and by whom' the decision is taken — and the paragraph then contrasts a driver's split-second choice with one made 'months earlier, in an office'.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [4]?
questions.explanation: B poses the question of blame, which the next sentences answer with the company, the programmers and the regulation each passing it on. E mentions insurers, whom the paragraph never returns to.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [5]?
questions.explanation: G gives concrete examples of humans driving 'unequally', and 'such data' in the next sentence refers to records of that behaviour.

questions.q: What is the writer's main argument?
options: Self-driving cars should not be permitted until the public agrees on whom they should protect.
Philosophers understand the technology better than the people who build it.
The real ethical problem is not the crash dilemma but the way decisions and responsibility have been relocated.
Engineers have solved the ethical problems that philosophers still worry about.
questions.explanation: The writer sets aside the swerve dilemma ('located it in the wrong place') and argues that the change lies in reflex becoming policy, responsibility being scattered, and bias being copied into code.

questions.q: What does the writer imply about the survey results mentioned in the first paragraph?
options: They were conducted mainly among engineers.
They reveal more about people's self-interest than about ethics.
They show that most people would refuse to travel in a self-driving car.
They have shifted noticeably over the past decade.
questions.explanation: The phrase 'with tedious consistency' and the finding that people want other cars to sacrifice passengers but their own to protect them show the writer regards the surveys as exposing self-interest, not moral insight.

questions.q: The writer believes the engineers' objection settles the ethical debate.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The writer reports the engineers' view but immediately adds that 'the philosophers are not wrong that something has changed', and spends the rest of the passage on what that is.
